**The model's input pieces need not match the units required by the task.** If “strawberry” is represented by one or a few subword tokens, counting its letters requires reconstructing the spelling and performing a character-level operation. Counting tokens is not counting r's. The correct count is three: one in “str” and two in “rry.” [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226)

Arithmetic has a related alignment problem. To add 98 and 7, the ones column produces 15: write 5 and carry 1. The tens column then becomes 10, producing 105. A learned representation of arbitrary multi-digit chunks may not expose that same column structure consistently across numbers of different lengths.

Single-digit tokenization supplies a consistent basic unit. Right-to-left grouping aligns chunks from the least-significant end, where ordinary addition starts, so unequal-length numbers have more consistent boundaries. These choices make useful structure easier to learn; they do not prove that a model learned an exact algorithm or will generalize to much longer inputs.

For an application requiring exact results, use a validated arithmetic or string operation. Specify what “character” means for Unicode: bytes, code points, and user-perceived graphemes can differ. Evaluate unfamiliar spellings and number lengths, not just examples commonly seen during training. A tokenizer change is an inductive bias; external computation is a separate reliability mechanism.

**Technical details and references.**

Subword tokens hide character boundaries: a word may be one token or several chunks, so counting letters requires recovering and operating on its spelling rather than counting input tokens. Arithmetic similarly depends on digit alignment, carries, and place value, which arbitrary multi-digit chunks can obscure. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226)

Single-digit tokenization exposes consistent units; right-to-left grouping can align least-significant digits and carries. These inductive biases may help but do not guarantee algorithmic generalization to longer numbers. “Strawberry” has three r's regardless of its tokenizer representation.

For exact tasks, execute a deterministic string/counting or arithmetic operation and validate its input. Benchmark across lengths and unusual characters, including Unicode normalization; apparent gains on familiar number lengths can conceal failure on distribution shifts.
